goal: From the README alone, someone who meets the product for the first time starts using it only when it serves their work.

parts.what: The product's name first, and under it one sentence that says what kind of thing the product is and what it does.
The paragraph after the summary: whom the product is for and what they gain with it.
After the gain: the idea that makes the gain possible, in a paragraph; where the idea has parts, how they fit together, and each part with what it is and what it ensures for the reader.
At the end of the opening, before anything about installing: each thing the product does not do that a reader might expect of it, set apart so the reader sees it as what the product does not do.
Each thing that must be in place before installing.
The steps that install the product.
One run of the use most readers come for, step by step, each step with what the product shows, up to the result.

One figure of the user, the product's parts and the things they pass, each shown by its name only, and the action or intent of each toward another, so a reader sees at a glance how the opening's promises are kept. Under it stand only the points and what the figure cannot show.
Where to read next: for users, the documents for fuller use; apart from them, for those who change the product, the development documents.
The license's name, linked to its full text.

benefits.what: When a colleague asks what the product is, can the reader answer in one sentence that tells them what it does?
Reading the gain, can the reader tell what the product would let them do, and so whether it is for them?
When a colleague asks why this product and not another way of doing the same work, can the reader name what it does differently that brings the gain?
Before installing, can the reader tell what the product does not do that they might have expected of it?
After the walkthrough, can the reader tell that the product would give them, on work of their own, the gain the opening promised?
Starting with nothing set up, can the reader get the walkthrough's result by the README's steps alone?
For each gain and the idea, can the reader see in the figure of how the product works how the product keeps it?
When the reader needs more than the README gives, such as fuller use or a change to the product, can they tell from it where to read next?
Can the reader tell from the README the terms on which they and their team may use the product?
Reading from the top, does the reader find each answer just when they come to need it, so they can stop as soon as they have what they came for?

practices.thinking: The sentence names the kind of thing the product is and what it does, in words the reader already uses, so they can say it again to a colleague.
steps: Write one sentence on its own line under the title, such as "<Name> is a <kind> that <does what>.", saying what the product does with no feature names or mechanisms.
Ask whether a colleague who hears only the sentence could say what the product does; if not, replace each vague or praising word with what the product does.
